newsitem.title: RUSSIA: 17 wounded, no one dead in Ossetia grenade attack.
newsitem.headline: 17 wounded, no one dead in Ossetia grenade attack.

text.p: Seventeen people were wounded in a grenade attack on a bus carrying Ingush refugees in Russia's turbulent North Caucasus region on Thursday, a spokesman for Ingush President Ruslan Aushev said.

He said no one was killed, denying an earlier report from local authorities that at least two people had died as the bus, returning from Ingushetia to neighbouring North Ossetia, was targeted with grenade launchers.

"Fresh reports from the scene have no information about people killed in the bus. But all 17 have been wounded and 12 of them are in hospital in serious condition," said Manlis Chakhkiyev, the regional president's spokesman.
"An 11-year-old girl is in an especially serious state. Her arms are being amputated at the hospital," he said.

It was not clear who carried out the attack, which occurred in North Ossetia 15 km (10 miles) from the Ingush border. An armed conflict between North Ossetia and Ingushetia in 1992 killed about 200 people and sparked a huge flow of Ingush refugees.

More than 20 attacks against Ingush refugees returning to their homes in Prigorodny district, controlled by North Ossetia, have been committed in the last month, raising ethnic tension in the North Caucasus.
The Ingush side has pinned blame for the attacks on North Ossetians.

Aushev told the Russian ness agency Interfax on Thursday he saw the attacks as a concerted attempt to destabilise the situation and urged Russian President Boris Yeltsin to introduce direct presidential rule.
Earlier this week, Aushev cabled Yeltsin warning him that tensions with the neighbouring region had increased sharply and appealing for him to impose direct rule from Moscow.
"Ingushetia urges Russia to intervene in this conflict," the spokesman said.
Itar-Tass quoted a senior official at Russia's Security Council as saying it planned to meet soon to discuss the acute problems of the North Caucasus region.
The seeds of the conflict lie in the deportation of the entire Ingush people to Central Asia by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin during World War Two.
Much of their land was taken over by Ossetians but, in the early 1990s, Ingushis tried to return. Fighting erupted, causing a serious refugee problem in tiny Ingushetia.
